title: Integration — Building an Authentic Nonverbal Self
hook: After learning to read everyone else, the last task is to let your own body say what is true, and to be readable without performing.
why:
This book has spent most of its length teaching you to read other people: their baselines, their clusters, their changes, their contexts, and the many ways in which a body can be misread because of culture, class, race, size, age, disability, faith or the performance of manhood itself. It has also warned, again and again, against the temptation to treat that reading as a tool for control.

There is a risk in all this study. A man who has learned to watch bodies closely can start watching his own too closely, staging his gestures, managing his face, rehearsing his posture, until he looks like someone acting the part of himself. People notice. Performance, however polished, reads as performance.

This final chapter turns the book's methods inward. It asks what authenticity means and what it does not, how to bring words and body into line, how to know your own baseline, how to build a personal protocol you will actually use, and how to become readable rather than impressive. It is the end of the book, and the beginning of the practice.

teach.h: What the book has been teaching.
teach.p:
Strip away the detail, and the method of this book comes down to a handful of habits. Know the baseline: what a body does when nothing is happening. Look for clusters, not single signs. Read change rather than state. Weigh context before meaning. Ask what would prove you wrong, and look for it. Hold conclusions lightly, and confirm them in words.

Around the method sit a few commitments. Reading people is not a way to manipulate them. Nonverbal cues are not a lie detector; the evidence that anyone can reliably spot deception from the body is weak, as Part I's chapter on deception showed. Nonverbal signs are not a diagnosis; a reader who suspects illness or crisis should encourage professional help, not play doctor. And the people least like you are the ones you are most likely to misread, which is why this part of the book exists.

These habits apply as well to the body you know best. You also have a baseline, clusters of habits, signs that change under pressure and contexts that shape what your body says. You can be misread, and you can misread yourself.

The figure here stands at rest, shoulders level, arms loose: the reference posture from the very first chapter, the line every other reading is measured against. Your own version of it is where this chapter begins.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if the method applied only to other people. A man's own body has a baseline, habits and stress signals of its own, and is subject to the same misreadings.

teach.p:
In 2008 Alex Wood and colleagues developed a short measure of authenticity built on the ideas of the psychologist Carl Rogers. They described three parts. Self-alienation is the sense of not knowing yourself, or feeling out of touch with the real you. Authentic living is behaving in line with your values and beliefs. Accepting external influence is the degree to which you go along with what others expect, even against your own sense of what is right.

People who scored higher on authenticity, with less self-alienation, more authentic living and less acceptance of external influence, tended to report higher self-esteem, greater well-being and less stress. The direction of cause is not settled by such studies, but the link is consistent with much other research.

Several chapters in this part described men whose bodies are constantly managed for an audience: masking, covering, code-switching, performing manhood. Each carries a cost that looks very like self-alienation. The answer is not to stop adapting, which is impossible and often unkind, but to keep a clear line between what you adapt and what you are, and to have places where the line can disappear.

The figure here breathes easily, shoulders down, chest soft. It is how the body tends to look when it is not bracing against being seen.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if feeling true to yourself had no link with well-being. Wood and colleagues found that higher authenticity was associated with higher self-esteem and well-being and lower stress.

teach.p:
A common idea is that being authentic means doing whatever comes naturally: saying every thought, showing every feeling, refusing to adapt. Research suggests otherwise. In 2010 William Fleeson and Joshua Wilt asked people to report, several times a day, how they were behaving and how true to themselves they felt. People felt most authentic when they were acting in an outgoing, kind, conscientious, calm and open way, whatever their usual personality. Introverts, for example, felt more like themselves when they were acting extraverted, not less.

Later work by Constantine Sedikides and colleagues suggested that feeling authentic is less about matching your habits and more about being at your best: acting on your values, connecting with others, feeling competent. A man who stays calm in a crisis, though his heart is racing, may feel more himself than one who panics, because calm is who he wants to be.

For the body, this means that authenticity is not the absence of control. Settling your breath before a hard conversation, softening your face when someone is upset, sitting down to talk to someone in a wheelchair: none of these is fake. They are your values made visible.

The figure here stands open, hands relaxed, weight even. It is not a pose struck for effect. It is what a body tends to do when its owner has decided to be present.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people felt most authentic when they acted on every impulse. Fleeson and Wilt found that people felt most authentic when acting in kind, conscientious and emotionally stable ways, whatever their traits.
teach.pullQuote: Authenticity is not the absence of control. It is your values made visible.

teach.p:
Carl Rogers used the word congruence for a state in which what a person feels, what he knows he feels and what he expresses all line up. He saw it as one of the conditions for any helping relationship to work. In nonverbal terms, congruence is when the words, the voice, the face and the body say the same thing.

Part IV's chapter on stage presence made the case that the speakers people trust are rarely the most theatrical; they are the ones whose bodies look as if they belong to the person talking. Its chapter on leadership argued that people follow leaders whose bodies say two things at once: I can handle this, and I am on your side. Both are descriptions of congruence.

Incongruence is easy to produce and hard to hide. A smile that arrives a beat late, a gesture placed for effect, a confident voice over a braced body, words of care delivered while looking at the door: observers may not know what is wrong, but they feel that something is.

The practical rule is to let the body follow the meaning rather than staging it. Decide what you mean, say it as plainly as you can, and let your hands and face do what they do. The figure here gestures with an open hand, the kind of movement that arrives on its own when someone is explaining something they care about.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if audiences did not notice mismatches between words and body. Earlier chapters described how readily people detect a staged gesture or a late smile, even when they cannot say what is wrong.

teach.p:
The first chapter of this book argued that a gesture means nothing until you know what that body does when nothing is happening. The same is true of your own body. Most men have a vague idea of how they come across and a poor idea of their actual habits.

There are simple ways to learn. Watch a recording of yourself in an ordinary conversation, with the sound off, and then with it on. Ask two people who know you well what you do when you are tired, stressed, bored or pleased, and listen without arguing. Notice where tension gathers in your body at the end of a hard day: jaw, shoulders, hands, stomach.

Psychologists use the term self-concept clarity for how clearly and consistently a person understands himself. In research by Jennifer Campbell and colleagues, people with clearer self-concepts tended to have higher self-esteem and to be less anxious. Knowing your own baseline is a bodily version of the same clarity. It lets you notice your own changes, and it makes you less likely to be thrown by someone else's misreading of you.

The figure here sits at rest, back against the chair, hands on the thighs, feet flat. Your own version of this posture, and what it looks like on a good day and a bad one, is worth knowing as well as you know your own handwriting.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people already knew their own nonverbal habits well. Most people are surprised by recordings of themselves, and those who know them well can usually name habits they had not noticed.

teach.p:
Part I closed with a synthesis that described expertise in reading people as a written procedure you trust because you have watched it fail. Part VI described how to wire such a protocol to the moments that need it. The same idea can be turned inward.

A personal protocol for your own body need not be long. It might list three signs that you are under more stress than you realise: a clenched jaw, a faster voice, a habit of interrupting. It might list three responses: a slow breath out, dropping the shoulders, sitting back. And it might list a few commitments: to ask before helping, to sit down to talk with anyone sitting, to confirm in words what a nod seemed to mean, to never use what you can read to manipulate.

The protocol is not a script for how to look. It is a set of checks that let your body return to its baseline when pressure pulls it away, and a set of commitments that keep your reading of others honest. Write it on one page. Review it after hard conversations. Change it when it fails.

The figure here breathes low and slow, hand on the belly. Of all the items in a personal protocol, a breath like this is the one most men find they use most.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if writing down and rehearsing responses made no difference to behaviour under pressure. Part VI described evidence that specific, practised plans are more likely to be carried out than good intentions.

teach.p:
Part VI ended with the idea of the quiet body: that the last skill is not seeing more in other people but disturbing them less, until your attention feels to them like a place to rest. This book ends with a companion idea. The aim is not to control how you are read. It is to be readable: to let what is true show, and to trust others to read it.

Readable men are not unguarded with everyone. They choose where to be open. But where they are open, their bodies match their words, their concern shows on their faces, their pleasure reaches their eyes, and their tiredness is allowed to look like tiredness. People relax around them because nothing needs to be decoded.

The same spirit applies to how you read others. Every chapter in this part showed how easily a body is misread when the reader brings the wrong map. The best readers hold their maps lightly, ask more than they assume, and give people the benefit of the doubt that they would want for themselves.

The figures here sit side by side on a bench, one leaning forward, the other beside him. Nobody is performing. It is where this book has been heading all along: two people, reading each other with care, and letting themselves be read.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if performance were more trusted than readability. The chapters on presence and leadership described how audiences trust speakers and leaders whose bodies match their words over those who stage their effects.

poseGallery.doCaption: Letting the hands follow the point
poseGallery.annotation: A gesture placed for effect usually reads as placed. Decide what you mean, and let your hands follow.

poseGallery.doCaption: Breathing, and letting yourself be seen
poseGallery.annotation: Where it is safe, let the guard drop. People relax around a body that is not bracing.
Presence is not a technique. It is attention that the other person can feel.

poseGallery.doCaption: Looking up, turned towards her, meaning it
poseGallery.annotation: When words and body disagree, people believe the body. Let your body say what your words mean.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Studying a partner's face for clues
poseGallery.annotation: The people closest to you deserve the gentlest reading. At home, let the attention rest.

caseStudy:
Arjun, forty-five, works in sales and has always been good with people. Two years ago he became fascinated by body language, read everything he could find, and began to apply it. He mirrored clients' postures, steepled his hands in negotiations, held eye contact for a counted three seconds and checked his own stance in shop windows.

For a while it seemed to work. Then his wife, Priya, told him over dinner that talking to him had started to feel like watching someone act. A long-standing client said, half joking, that Arjun had become very polished lately. And Arjun noticed that he was exhausted after meetings in a way he had not been before, and that he could not remember what clients had said because he had been so busy watching himself.

He stopped the techniques for a month. Instead, he wrote a one-page protocol. Three signs of his own stress: talking fast, leaning in too far, tapping his pen. Three responses: a slow breath out, sitting back, putting the pen down. Three commitments: listen before reading, say what he means plainly, and never use what he notices to push someone into a decision.

Within a few weeks, Priya said that he seemed like himself again. The client who had called him polished told him he seemed more relaxed. Arjun noticed that he remembered conversations better, and that he read people more accurately when he was not also performing for them.

He still notices bodies; he cannot stop. But he now thinks of what he learned less as a set of techniques and more as a habit of attention, pointed mostly outward, and gentle when it turns in.
observe: Notice, in your next important conversation, whether you are attending to the other person or to how you are coming across.
Notice moments when your words and your body say different things, and what you were feeling at the time.
Notice the people you find most readable, and what they do that makes them so.
Notice your own baseline at the end of a good day and a hard one, and where the difference shows.

drills.name: Watch Yourself
steps: Record yourself in an ordinary conversation, with permission from the other person.
Watch it once with the sound off, noting your posture, gestures and face.
Watch it again with the sound on, noting where words and body match and where they do not.
Write down three habits you had not noticed before.
variations: Record yourself in two different settings, such as a work meeting and a family meal, and compare your habits in each.
Watch a recording of yourself listening rather than speaking, and notice what your face does when someone else is talking.
After watching, choose one habit you like and want to keep, as well as one you want to change.

drills.name: Ask Two People
steps: Choose two people who know you well and whom you trust.
Ask each what your body does when you are stressed, bored, pleased and tired.
Compare their answers with your own picture of yourself.
variations: Ask a third person from a different part of your life, such as a colleague if the first two were family, and compare all three answers.
Ask the two people what they think you do when you are happy, and notice whether you recognise it.
Thank each person afterwards, and tell them one specific thing that their answer taught you about yourself.

drills.name: One-Page Protocol
steps: Write down three signs that you are under more stress than you realise.
Write down three responses that bring you back to your baseline.
Write down three commitments for how you will read and treat others.
Keep the page where you will see it, and review it after hard conversations.
Revise it after a month, keeping what worked and changing what did not.
variations: Share your protocol with one trusted person and ask them to tell you when they see your stress signs.
Add one commitment about how you will treat yourself when you notice the signs, not just others.
Write a version of the protocol for home as well as one for work, if your signs differ between them.

drills.name: Let It Follow
steps: Before your next explanation or presentation, decide exactly what you mean to say.
Do not plan any gestures, postures or expressions.
Say it as plainly as you can, and let your body do what it does.
Afterwards, ask one listener how you came across.
variations: Try the drill in a difficult conversation as well as an explanation, deciding only what you want to say and letting your body follow.
After a conversation where you let your body follow, ask yourself whether you remember more of what the other person said than usual.
Notice one moment in the conversation when you started to plan a gesture, and simply let it go.

quiz.q: A colleague says being authentic means expressing every feeling and impulse as it comes, whatever the setting. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right, since any control over what you show is a kind of lie to the people around you
People tend to feel most authentic acting on their values and at their best, not unfiltered
Authenticity is a myth, since every expression is a performance of one kind or another
He is right, but only at home, since workplaces require every feeling to be kept hidden
quiz.explain: Fleeson and Wilt found that people felt most authentic when acting in kind, conscientious and stable ways. Settling your breath or softening your face can be your values made visible.

quiz.q: What did Fleeson and Wilt find in their 2010 study of authenticity?
options: People felt most authentic acting outgoing, kind and calm, whatever their usual personality
Introverts felt least authentic whenever they acted in a more outgoing or sociable way than usual
People felt most authentic when their behaviour exactly matched their usual traits
Feeling authentic had no link at all with how people were behaving at the time
quiz.explain: Across repeated reports, people felt most true to themselves when acting in outgoing, agreeable, conscientious, stable and open ways. That held even for introverts.

quiz.q: Which three parts did Wood and colleagues use to describe authenticity?
options: Confidence, charisma and composure, each measured in the way that a person stands and moves
Honesty, humility and humour, each judged by close friends and family members
Self-alienation, authentic living and accepting external influence on behaviour
Eye contact, open posture and a steady voice, each rated by trained observers
quiz.explain: Wood and colleagues built their measure on Carl Rogers's ideas. Higher authenticity was linked with higher self-esteem and well-being and with lower stress.

quiz.q: What is the first step this book recommends before interpreting any signal, in others or in yourself?
options: Look for the single most telling gesture, and interpret that one before the others
Decide quickly what the person is feeling, and then look for signs to confirm it
Compare the person with a general norm for people of their age, sex and culture
Establish a baseline of what the body does when nothing in particular is happening
quiz.explain: A gesture means nothing until you know what that body does at rest. The same applies to your own body: knowing your baseline lets you notice your own changes.

quiz.q: After studying body language, you find yourself managing every gesture you make, and a friend says you seem stiff and rehearsed. What fits this chapter best?
options: Practise the gestures harder, until they become smooth enough to pass for natural
Step back from managing gestures, and let your body follow what you actually mean
Stop reading other people altogether, since the study has clearly done you harm
Ask the friend to tell you which gestures look the most staged, and drop only those
quiz.explain: Staged gestures tend to read as staged. Deciding what you mean and letting the body follow restores congruence, and frees attention for the other person.

quiz.q: You are about to give your team difficult news about job cuts. What fits this chapter best?
options: Hold a confident smile throughout, so that the team is not unsettled by the news
Keep a completely blank face, so that nobody can read anything into your expression
Settle your breath, say it plainly, and let your face show the concern you feel
Rehearse a set of reassuring gestures, so that your body sends a calm message
quiz.explain: Congruence means words, voice and face saying the same thing. A forced smile over bad news reads as false; plain words and visible concern are trusted.

quiz.q: What did Sedikides and colleagues suggest that feeling authentic is mostly about?
options: Matching your usual habits as closely as possible in every situation
Being at your best: acting on your values, connecting with others and feeling competent
Expressing every feeling and impulse as it comes, whatever the setting
Refusing to adapt your behaviour to other people's expectations at any time, whatever they are
quiz.explain: Sedikides and colleagues suggested that feeling authentic is less about matching your habits and more about being at your best: acting on your values, connecting with others and feeling competent. A man who stays calm in a crisis because it matters to him is being himself.

quiz.q: A father says "That's brilliant, well done" to his daughter's news while looking at his phone, and she goes upstairs upset. What fits this chapter best?
options: Explain to her that the words were what mattered, since he meant every one of them
Put the phone down, turn towards her, and say it again so that his body matches his words
Leave it, since teenagers often overreact and she will have forgotten all about it by the morning
Send her a message saying well done, so that she has it in writing to read again
quiz.explain: When words and body disagree, people tend to believe the body. Congruence, words, face and body saying the same thing, is what lets the praise land as meant.

quiz.q: Someone says that people cannot really tell when your words and your body do not match. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That incongruence is easy to produce and hard to hide, and people often sense it without knowing why
That nobody notices incongruence, so it does not matter what your body does while you speak
That only trained experts can detect incongruence, and ordinary people never notice it
That incongruence only matters in formal settings such as interviews and presentations
quiz.explain: A smile that arrives a beat late, a gesture placed for effect or a confident voice over a worried face are easy to produce and hard to hide. People sense that something is wrong, even when they cannot say what.

reflection.prompt: Look back over everything you have learned in this book, and think of one specific way your own body is most often misread, or most often out of line with what you mean. Describe the situation, what your body does, and what you are actually feeling at the time. Then write the first three lines of your own personal protocol: one sign of your stress, one response that brings you back, and one commitment for how you will read and treat other people.
reflection.guidance: This is the last reflection in the book, and it is meant to be practical. Keep the protocol short enough to remember under pressure. It is not a verdict on who you are, but a first draft that you will revise as you watch it succeed and fail. Return to it in a month and change what did not work.

failureMode: The first failure is to turn the study of bodies into a performance of your own, staging gestures until you look like someone acting the part of yourself. The second is to confuse authenticity with having no filter, and treat every impulse as true. The third is to let words and body drift apart, so that people sense something is wrong without knowing what. The fourth is to never learn your own baseline, and so be thrown by your own stress signals or by other people's misreadings. The fifth is to keep a protocol in your head rather than on paper, where it can be tested and revised. And the sixth is to forget the commitments that sit around the method: no manipulation, no lie detection, no diagnosis, and humility toward the people you are most likely to misread.

moreCases.title: The reader who could not stop reading
moreCases.scene:
Adam, thirty-two, is a nurse, and over the past year he has read almost everything he can find about body language, including most of this book.
  He is good at it. He notices when patients are frightened before they say so, and colleagues have started asking him to sit in on difficult
  conversations with families.

  At home, it has become a problem. He reads his partner, Ellie, constantly: the tightness in her jaw when she comes in from work, the way she crosses
  her arms during a phone call with her mother, the half-second pause before she says she is fine. He comments on what he sees, kindly, and asks
  questions. "You look tense. Is it your mum again?" "You touched your neck then. Are you worried about something?" Twice, he has suggested that her
  low mood might be the start of depression and that she should see someone.

  One evening, after he asks why she frowned at a text message, Ellie puts her phone down and says, quietly, that she feels as if she is living with
  a detective. She says she has started to manage her face around him, which she has never had to do with anyone before.

  Adam is stung. He had thought he was being attentive. Then he remembers the first chapter of this book, about baselines, and realises that he has
  never once asked Ellie what her own baseline is.

He also realises that he has been telling colleagues about Ellie's signals, as examples of what he has learned, and that she would be mortified if she knew.

He has also, he realises, been reading his friends at the pub, his sister at Sunday lunch and his own father on the phone, and he cannot remember the last time he simply enjoyed a conversation without analysing it.

Ellie tells him, too, that she had stopped mentioning her mother, because every mention led to a conversation about what her face had done while she talked about her.
moreCases.misread:
Adam read Ellie's small signals as information to be decoded and commented on, and read his own comments as care. Ellie read them as being watched and analysed, which made her start to manage her face around the person she most wanted to be relaxed with.

He also read his own expertise as a reason to trust his readings of Ellie over her own account, which is the opposite of what the book had taught him.

He also read Ellie's growing quietness, in the weeks before she spoke up, as a sign of the low mood he had worried about, when much of it was a response to being watched.
moreCases.betterRead:
This chapter's failure mode lists, among the commitments that sit around the method, no diagnosis and humility towards the people you read, and it describes the aim as attention pointed mostly outward and gentle when it turns in. Adam's attention had become scrutiny. Part VI ended with the idea of the quiet body: that the last skill is disturbing others less, until your attention feels like a place to rest. The better approach was to stop narrating what he saw and start asking, openly and less often: "How was your day?" and then listening to the words. He stopped commenting on her gestures. When he was genuinely worried, he said so plainly, once, and left the decision to her. Within a month, Ellie said that home felt like home again. Adam kept reading people at work, where it helped. At home, he let it rest.

Ellie also told him, months later, that she had started telling him things she would not have mentioned before, because she no longer felt she was being studied.

He also apologised to Ellie, simply, for making her feel watched, which mattered to her more than the change itself.

moreCases.title: The introvert at the wedding
moreCases.scene:
Nina, twenty-nine, is a quiet, thoughtful software tester, and she is maid of honour at her best friend's wedding. She dreads the speech. She is an
  introvert, prefers small groups and has always believed that standing up in front of a hundred people and being funny is simply not who she is. She
  considers asking someone else to give it.

  Her friend, the bride, Rosa, says that she does not need Nina to be anyone else, only to say what she thinks. Nina writes a speech about their
  friendship, practises it aloud, standing, five times, and on the day stands up with her heart pounding.

  Something surprising happens. A few sentences in, the room laughs at a story about the two of them getting lost on a school trip, and Nina finds
  herself enjoying it. She looks up, catches Rosa's eye, pauses for the laugh, and goes on more warmly than she had planned. By the end, she is moved and
  so is the room. Afterwards, three strangers tell her it was the best speech of the day.

  That night, in her hotel room, she is exhausted and also, oddly, happy. She tells her sister on the phone that she felt more like herself giving that
  speech than she has in years, and that she does not understand why.

She had also spent the morning of the wedding hiding in the hotel garden, rehearsing under her breath, convinced that she would freeze. Rosa had found her there and told her she did not have to be funny.

She also notices, at the reception, that she talks easily to Rosa's grandmother and two strangers at her table, and that she is not pretending to enjoy it. She is enjoying it.

Her father, at the reception, tells her that he had no idea she could do that, and she tells him that neither had she.
moreCases.misread:
Nina read her own introversion as a fixed rule about what she could be, and read the outgoing, funny speech as a performance that would not be her. The experience of giving it contradicted both readings.

Her sister, on the phone, read Nina's confusion as surprise at having enjoyed it, which was part of it. The rest was a new picture of herself that would take time to settle.

Rosa, who had known Nina for twenty years, read her far more accurately, as a quiet woman with a great deal to say about the people she loved, given the right occasion.

She also read the exhaustion afterwards, at first, as proof that the speech had not really been her, when it was simply the cost of giving a lot.
moreCases.betterRead:
Fleeson and Wilt found that people felt most authentic when they were acting in an outgoing, kind, conscientious, calm and open way, whatever their usual personality; introverts felt more like themselves when acting extraverted, not less. Sedikides and colleagues suggested that feeling authentic is less about matching your habits and more about being at your best. Nina's speech was not a performance of someone else. It was her, speaking about something she cared about, to people she loved, at her best. Her exhaustion afterwards was real too, and worth respecting: she slept late, skipped the brunch and spent the next day quietly. The better reading of herself, which she took from the wedding, was that authenticity is not a narrow box but a direction: acting on what she values, in whatever register the moment needs, and then resting.

She also kept the outgoing side for occasions that mattered to her, and stopped apologising for the quiet side the rest of the time.

At Rosa's first anniversary party, a year later, Nina gave a second, shorter speech, without being asked, and enjoyed it just as much.

moreCases.title: The father who said well done to his phone
moreCases.scene:
Colin, fifty, is a project manager who works long hours, and he loves his daughter, Molly, fifteen, more than he can say. One evening Molly comes
  into the kitchen, glowing, to tell him that she has been picked for the county hockey team. Colin is sitting at the table answering emails on his
  phone. He looks up for a second, says "That's brilliant, well done, love," and looks back down at the screen. He means every word.

  Molly stands there for a moment. Then she says "Thanks," flatly, and goes upstairs. Colin does not notice the flatness. He is pleased for her and
  thinks the conversation went well.

  Later, his wife, Jo, tells him that Molly is upset. She had run all the way home from the bus to tell him first. She told her mother that Dad didn't
  care, that he had barely looked up.

  Colin is shocked. He had said exactly the right words. He goes upstairs and knocks on Molly's door. She is lying on her bed with her headphones in.
  He asks if he can come in, and sits on the end of the bed, and puts his phone face down on the floor, where she can see it.

He also realises, sitting on the end of the bed, that he cannot remember the last time he put his phone down when one of his children came into a room.

Jo also mentions, gently, that their son has stopped telling Colin things at all, and that she had assumed Colin knew.

He also remembers his own father, who read the newspaper at the breakfast table every morning of Colin's childhood and said "Very good" to everything without lowering it.

Jo noticed, a few weeks after that evening, that their son had started sitting at the kitchen table while Colin cooked, talking about school, which he had not done for a year.
moreCases.misread:
Molly read her father's brief glance and his return to the screen as indifference, whatever his words said. Colin read his own words as the whole message, and did not notice that his body had said something quite different.

Jo, too, had read Colin's distraction for years as tiredness, and had stopped expecting more, which was a quieter cost of the same habit.

And he read his own pride as something Molly could feel through the words, when what she could see was the top of his head and the glow of a screen.

Molly's younger brother, watching from the doorway, read it the same way she did, and would have learned the same lesson.
moreCases.betterRead:
Carl Rogers used the word congruence for a state in which what a person feels and what he expresses line up, and this chapter describes incongruence, words and body saying different things, as easy to produce and hard to hide. When words and body disagree, people tend to believe the body. Colin's "well done" was true, and his eyes on the phone made it sound false. The better response, which he gave on the end of the bed, was to make his body match the words: phone down, turned towards her, eyes on her face, and the same sentence again, slowly. "I'm really proud of you. Tell me everything." Molly took her headphones out and told him about the trial, the goal she had scored and the coach who had picked her. Colin asked questions for twenty minutes. Afterwards he made a rule for himself: when someone he loved came in with news, the phone went face down first.

Molly noticed the phone face down on the floor before he said anything, and that, she told her mother later, was what made her take the headphones out.

moreCases.title: The protocol that failed in the moment
moreCases.scene:
Hamid, forty-four, leads a team of twelve at an insurance company, and after reading this book he wrote a one-page protocol, as the chapter
  suggests. Three signs that he is under more stress than he realises: talking fast, interrupting, a tight jaw. Three responses: a slow breath out,
  sitting back, putting his pen down. Three commitments: listen before deciding, say what he means plainly, and never use what he notices to push
  someone. He keeps it in his desk drawer.

  Two months later, in a meeting about a client complaint that has reached the chief executive, Hamid's protocol fails completely. He talks fast,
  interrupts three people, cuts off a junior colleague, Mia, who is trying to explain what happened, and leaves the meeting with his jaw aching. He
  realises on the way back to his desk that he did not think of the protocol once.

  That evening, he takes the page out of the drawer and reads it, and feels slightly foolish. It is all correct. None of it was there when he needed it.

  He remembers that Part VI described something about this: that a protocol needs to be wired to the moments that need it, or it stays in the drawer.
  He also remembers that Mia had been right about the complaint, and that he had not let her finish.

He also notices that the card he wrote for himself is still in its envelope in the drawer, unopened since the day he put it there.

His wife, when he tells her about the meeting, reminds him that the stillness and the fast talking always come when he is afraid of letting someone down, and that the chief executive's name had been on the complaint.

He also realises that the meeting was exactly the kind of moment he had written the protocol for, and that writing it had made him feel as if the work was done.
moreCases.misread:
Hamid read his own protocol as finished once it was written, and read the failure in the meeting as proof that he was bad at managing himself. Mia, cut off mid-sentence, read his interruptions as a judgment on her explanation.

He also read the protocol itself as a failure, when the failure was in how he had stored it.

His team, for their part, read his interruptions in the meeting as panic, and two of them stopped speaking for the rest of it, which meant that the solution Mia had been about to offer was not heard.

Mia, for her part, read the cut-off as a sign that her explanation was wrong, and nearly did not raise it again.
moreCases.betterRead:
This chapter describes a personal protocol as a set of checks that let you notice and correct yourself, not a script, and Part VI described how protocols must be wired to the moments that need them. A page in a drawer cannot interrupt a stress response in a heated meeting; a habit tied to a trigger can. Hamid's better approach was to revise the protocol, as the One-Page Protocol drill recommends after a month, and to make it usable in the moment. He wrote "Breathe. Sit back. Let them finish" on a card and put it inside the cover of the notebook he takes to every meeting. He agreed with his deputy that she would tap the table if he started interrupting. And he went to Mia the next morning, apologised for cutting her off and asked her to explain the complaint again. She did, and her explanation changed the firm's response to the client.

He also told his team, at the next meeting, that he had interrupted too much in the complaint meeting and was working on it, which made it easier for them to tell him when he did it again.

workedReading.title: Writing your own one-page protocol
workedReading.scene:
Nathan, thirty-eight, runs a small architecture practice with six staff, and he has finished reading this book. He has learned a great deal about reading others, and he suspects he knows less about how he himself comes across. His partner says he goes quiet and distant when he is stressed; one of his staff once told him he seemed annoyed in a meeting where he had been perfectly happy. He decides to write a one-page protocol, as this chapter suggests, and to base it on evidence rather than on his own picture of himself. He gives himself a fortnight to gather that evidence and an evening to write the page. He also decides that the protocol will be a set of checks, not a script for how to look, because the aim, as this chapter says, is to be readable rather than to perform.

He also remembers that this chapter describes the aim as being readable, not performing, and he wants his protocol to help him notice himself, not to manage how he looks.

He also remembers the client in last month's meeting who said he seemed annoyed, and wonders how many other people have read him that way without saying so.

He also notices that he is slightly afraid of what the evidence will show, which tells him that it is worth gathering.

He also decides that he will share the finished page with his partner, because she is the person most likely to notice when he forgets it.

steps.label: Gather evidence first
steps.text:
He uses the Watch Yourself drill, recording a client meeting with permission and watching it with the sound off. He notices that he folds his arms when he is thinking, frowns when he concentrates and rarely smiles until the end of a meeting. Then he uses the Ask Two People drill with his partner and a long-standing colleague. Both say the same thing: when he is stressed, he goes very still and very quiet, and his answers get shorter.

He also notices, watching the recording, that he leans forward and smiles much more when a client talks about the building they want than when they talk about the budget, which he had never realised.

He also notices that he interrupts his junior architect more than anyone else, which neither of the two people he asked had mentioned, and adds it to his list.

steps.label: Name three stress signs
steps.text:
From the evidence, he writes his three signs: going quiet and still, giving one-word answers, and a frown that stays when there is nothing to frown at. He notes that none of these is what he would have guessed. He had thought that stress made him louder. This is why the chapter insists on learning your own baseline from others, not only from yourself.

He also writes down, separately, the signs that he is happy and relaxed, so that he knows what his baseline looks like on a good day.

He also writes down the situations in which the signs appear most often: client meetings about money, and Friday afternoons when he is tired.

He also notices that each sign on his list is something other people saw before he did, which is a useful reminder of how little of himself he can see from inside.

steps.label: Name three resets
steps.text:
He writes three responses that bring him back towards his baseline: one slow breath out, letting his shoulders drop; asking a question rather than answering in one word; and, when he can, standing up and walking to the window for a moment. He tests each one during the fortnight and keeps the ones that work.

He also notices that the resets work best early. Once the stillness has fully set in, it takes much longer to come back.

He also notes that one reset he had expected to work, counting to five before answering, made him seem even more distant, and drops it.

He also notes that the breath works in any setting, which is why it goes first on the card.

steps.label: Write three commitments
steps.text:
He writes three commitments for how he will read and treat others: to read change against each person's baseline rather than his own; to ask in words before acting on a reading, especially with people least like him; and never to use what he notices to push anyone into a decision they would not otherwise make. He notices that the third one is the one he would most like his staff to hold him to.

He also writes a commitment about himself: to say "I'm stressed, it's not you" when he notices the signs, so that others do not misread them.

He also writes one commitment about his staff: to ask each of them, once a quarter, how he comes across to them, and to listen.

He also keeps the commitments short enough to remember in a meeting, because a commitment he cannot recall in the moment is not much use.

steps.label: Wire it to moments
steps.text:
He does not put the page in a drawer. He writes the three resets on a card inside his meeting notebook, and he asks his partner and his colleague to tell him, gently, when they see the stillness setting in. He links the first reset to the moment a meeting gets tense, so that the breath becomes a habit tied to a trigger rather than a resolution.

He also puts a copy of the page on the inside of his kitchen cupboard, where he will see it every morning.

He also sets a reminder on his phone for the review, so that the page does not quietly become a piece of paper in a drawer.

steps.label: Test and revise after a month
steps.text:
After a month, he reviews the page. Two resets work; the walk to the window is impractical in most meetings, so he replaces it with putting his pen down. He adds a fourth stress sign that his colleague noticed: he stops making eye contact with junior staff. He also notices that he has been reading his staff more carefully, and asking more.

He also asks his partner and colleague whether the protocol has made any difference, and listens to their answers without arguing.

He also notices that the act of reviewing the page has become a small monthly conversation with himself, which he has come to look forward to.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
Six months later, the colleague who once thought he was annoyed tells him that he has become much easier to read. His partner says the stillness still comes, but that he notices it sooner and says, "I'm a bit stressed, it's not you," which helps. Nathan keeps the page on his desk and revises it every few months. He thinks of it, he says, as a map of himself, drawn by other people, that he keeps correcting.

He also gives a blank copy of the drill to each of his staff, without asking them to share what they write, in case any of them want to try it.

He also notices that one of his staff has started keeping a page of her own, and that she asks him, one day, what his three signs are. He tells her.

moreFailures.title: Reading the people closest to you like case studies
moreFailures.body:
After learning to read bodies, many people turn the skill on the people they live with, and it can feel like care. It often lands as surveillance, as Adam found with Ellie. Narrating someone's gestures back to them, "You touched your neck, are you anxious?", asking about every pause and frown, or suggesting that their mood is a sign of illness, makes them feel watched and analysed in the one place they most want to be relaxed. They may start managing their faces around you, which is the opposite of what you wanted. The people closest to you deserve the gentlest reading of all: their own baseline, learned over years; questions asked openly and not too often; and trust in what they tell you. Keep the sharper attention for work, for moments of real concern and for strangers you need to understand. At home, let it rest.

A good test is whether the person would describe your attention as warmth or as scrutiny. Ask them, if you are not sure.

If you have been doing it, tell the person, and ask what would feel better. The answer is often simpler than you expect.

moreFailures.title: Using authenticity as an excuse for unkindness
moreFailures.body:
"I'm just being honest," "That's just who I am," "I don't do fake." Each can be a sincere statement of values. Each can also be used to excuse rudeness, coldness or a refusal to consider how one's behaviour lands. This chapter argues that authentic is not the same as unfiltered: Fleeson and Wilt found that people feel most authentic when acting at their best, kindly, calmly and openly, not when acting on every impulse. A man who says a hurtful thing and calls it honesty, or who refuses to soften his manner for a grieving friend because softening is not "him", is mistaking a habit for a self. Authenticity means acting on your values, and kindness and consideration are usually among them. The question to ask is not "Is this what I feel?" but "Is this who I want to be?"

Honesty and kindness are not opposites. The most useful honesty is usually the kind that can be heard.

A good test is whether you would want someone you love to be "honest" with you in exactly the same way.

moreFailures.title: Waiting to feel authentic before acting
moreFailures.body:
Some people wait until a new way of behaving feels natural before they try it: they will be warmer with colleagues when warmth feels like them, they will speak up in meetings when it feels authentic, they will hug their sons when it no longer feels awkward. The feeling rarely comes first. Fleeson and Wilt's research, and Nina's wedding speech, suggest that acting on your values can itself produce the sense of being yourself, and that the awkwardness of a new behaviour usually fades with practice. Ray, in the previous chapter, did not wait to feel comfortable before hugging his son; he practised, and the comfort followed. Waiting for authenticity can mean waiting for ever. Choose the behaviour that fits the man you want to be, do it, and let the feeling catch up.

A useful question is: what would the man I want to be do here? Then do that, even if it feels strange at first.

It also helps to choose one small behaviour at a time, so that the change is manageable and the feeling has a chance to follow.

moreFailures.title: Treating the book as the last word
moreFailures.body:
A book like this one can tempt readers to treat its findings as rules and its methods as finished. They are neither. Many of the studies it reports are single studies, some with small samples; some have been challenged, and some will be overturned by better research, as the power posing chapter described. Every person you meet will, at some point, fail to fit the patterns described here. The method this book has tried to teach, know the baseline, look for clusters, read change, weigh context, ask what would prove you wrong and confirm in words, is designed to be humble about its own limits. Keep that humility. Keep reading, testing and revising, and keep asking the people you read whether you have got them right. The best readers of people are the ones who expect to be surprised.

It also helps to keep a note of the readings you got wrong, which are often more instructive than the ones you got right.

The best compliment a reader of people can receive is that the people they read felt understood, not studied.

questions.q: How can I tell whether I am performing rather than being myself?
questions.a:
A few signs suggest performance: you are watching yourself more than the other person, as Arjun found; you cannot remember what was said because you were managing your gestures; you feel exhausted after ordinary conversations; and people who know you well say you seem different, polished or like someone acting. Being yourself, by contrast, usually involves attention pointed outward, at the person and the subject, with your body following your point rather than leading it, as the Let It Follow drill rehearses. It does not mean having no adaptations; everyone adapts to settings. The question is whether your adaptations serve what you value and the people in front of you, or whether they serve an image you are trying to project.

Another test is to notice whether you could explain your behaviour to the person in front of you without embarrassment.

And performance is not always wrong. A eulogy or a wedding speech may need some staging; the question is whether the staging serves what you mean.

If you are not sure, ask a friend afterwards whether you seemed like yourself. They will usually know.

questions.q: Is it fake to adapt how I come across?
questions.a:
Not necessarily. Fleeson and Wilt found that people felt most authentic when acting in outgoing, kind, calm and open ways, whatever their usual personality, so adapting towards your best self can feel more like you, not less. The chapter on code-switching in this part describes adaptation as a skill when it is chosen and endorsed, and as a cost when it is constant and driven by fear. Wood and colleagues' measure of authenticity includes living in line with your values and not simply accepting others' expectations. So the question is not whether you adapt but why and how: whether the adaptation fits your values and the moment, as Nina's speech did, or whether it hides who you are to avoid judgment.

It also helps to notice whether you feel more yourself or less after a conversation in which you adapted.

And when an adaptation starts to feel like hiding, that is a sign to look again at why you are making it.

questions.q: What should go in my personal protocol?
questions.a:
Keep it to one page and base it on evidence. Three signs that you are under more stress than you realise, gathered from recordings of yourself and from people who know you, as Nathan did. Three responses that bring you back towards your baseline, tested in practice. And a few commitments for how you will read and treat others, such as reading change against each person's own baseline, asking before acting on a reading, and never using what you notice to manipulate. Then wire it to the moments that need it, as Part VI described: a card in your meeting notebook, a trusted person who will tell you when they see the signs. Review it after a month and revise it, keeping what works. It is a map of yourself that other people help you draw.

Keep it short enough to read in a minute. A protocol you never read is not a protocol.

It also helps to include one sign that you are at your best, so that the page reminds you what you are aiming for, not only what to avoid.

questions.q: How can I stop over-reading the people I live with?
questions.a:
Notice when you are narrating their gestures or asking about every small signal, and stop. Replace commentary with open questions asked less often: "How was your day?" rather than "You look tense." Listen to the words and take them at face value most of the time. Learn their baseline by living with them, not by analysing them, and remember that a frown at a text message is usually about the text message. When you are genuinely worried, say so plainly, once, and leave the decision to them, as Adam learned to do. Avoid suggesting that someone's mood is a sign of illness unless you are seriously concerned, and then encourage them to see a professional rather than offering your own view. The aim at home is to be a place where nobody has to manage their face.

It also helps to notice what the people you live with already do well, and to say so, which turns attention into appreciation.

It also helps to remember that the people you love are not puzzles to solve, but people to know, which takes years rather than glances.

And when you do notice something worrying, ask once, plainly, and trust the answer unless you have strong reason not to.

questions.q: What if my body gives away things I would rather keep private?
questions.a:
You are allowed to keep things private, and readable people are not unguarded with everyone. This chapter describes readable men as choosing where to be open. If someone notices that you seem tired or upset and asks, you can say so honestly without explaining: "I'm a bit off today, nothing I want to talk about, but thanks for asking." That is congruent, because your words match what your body is already showing, and it is private, because you have not shared the reason. What tends to cause trouble is denial, insisting that you are fine while everything about you says otherwise, which leaves people confused and sometimes worried. A short, true sentence lets your body and your words agree, and keeps the rest your own.

It also helps to have a few people with whom you do not need to keep anything private at all.

It also helps to notice which people you can be fully open with, and to make time for them.

questions.q: Where should I go from here?
questions.a:
Practise, and stay humble. Part VI of this book turns the methods described here into a discipline: reviewing yourself on video, calibrating across cultures, building protocols and wiring them to the moments that need them. Choose one drill from this part and do it this week. Keep your one-page protocol and revise it. Ask the people you read whether you have read them rightly, especially the people least like you. Treat every surprising reading as a chance to learn, and every finding in this book as a starting point rather than a rule. Above all, keep your attention pointed mostly outward, at the people in front of you, and let it be gentle when it turns in.

And remember that the point of all this was never to become an expert reader, but to understand and treat people better.

It also helps to return to the drills now and then, because habits drift, and what you notice about yourself changes as you change.

watch.title: Fred Rogers Acceptance Speech, 1997
watch.notice: Fred Rogers asks a room full of television stars for ten seconds of silence. Notice how little he performs, how his body matches his words, and how the room responds to someone who is simply readable.

watch.title: Good Will Hunting: It's Not Your Fault
watch.notice: A young man's guard finally gives way in front of his therapist. Watch the moment the performance of toughness stops, and what the older man does with his body to make that safe.

watch.title: The Power of Vulnerability
watch.notice: Brené Brown on vulnerability and connection. Listen for what she says about letting yourself be seen, and notice how her own delivery matches her words.

reviewPrompt: This week, write your one-page protocol, and in one important conversation let your body follow what you mean.
